title: The priest and the hunter
hookLine: the temple priest, and the hunter whose love Shiva saw
carry: the priest offers the form; you bring the heart
last: PRADAKSHINA — KEEP THE HOLY AT THE CENTER.

cards: In the hills of Kalahasti, in South India, the story goes, a temple priest came each morning to a lonely shrine of Shiva. He bathed the lingam, decorated it, chanted every verse exactly.
And each morning he found a mess: his flowers pushed aside, meat left on the stone, the lingam wet with water someone had carried in their mouth. The someone was a young hunter named Thinnan.
He knew no Sanskrit and no rules. He simply loved Shiva at first sight, and brought him what he had: water in his mouth, flowers from his own hair, the best meat from the hunt, tasted first.
Today: the priest, and the hunter.

teach.b: Shiva told the heartbroken priest in a dream: hide, and watch. The next day the hunter came, and the priest saw blood running from one eye of the lingam.
He cut out his own eye with an arrow and pressed it onto the bleeding one, and the bleeding stopped. Then the other eye began to bleed.
He set his foot on the spot so he wouldn't lose it, and raised the arrow to his second eye.

And Shiva's voice stopped him: stop, Kannappa. He's been Kannappa ever since, one of the sixty-three Tamil saints of Shiva in the Periya Puranam. The story doesn't throw out the priest: Shiva showed him the hunter's love.

teach.h: PUJARI — THE ONE WHO DOES THE PUJA.
teach.b: The priest's word is pujari, the one who does the puja.
In many temples only priests enter the inner shrine, and they care for the murti every day: bathing it, dressing it, feeding it, arti, by rules handed down for generations.
And when you bring an offering, he makes it for you.

He asks your name, often your family line, and sets them into the Sanskrit: who is offering, when, and why. That's the sankalpa. Then he recites the deity's names, often a hundred and eight, a flower with each: archana.
The priest keeps the form exact, and the offering is still yours. You don't have to know every word. Kannappa didn't know one, and Shiva received what he brought.
That love has a name: bhakti.

how: In Hindu temples, the pujari performs the daily rites for the deity (bathing, dressing, food offerings and arti), and on request performs archana on a devotee's behalf, opening with a sankalpa that names the worshipper; the Tamil saint Kannappa, the hunter who offered his own eye, is honored at the Kalahasti temple.

games.q: you're the priest at Kalahasti. every morning your perfect offerings are pushed aside and there's meat on the stone. Shiva tells you in a dream: hide and watch. what do you see?
o: a hunter who loves Shiva more than his own eyes.
another priest doing the rites wrong.
games.why: the hunter Thinnan gives his own eye when the lingam bleeds, and Shiva stops him: stop, Kannappa. the priest keeps the form; the love is what's offered.

practice: Take one small thing within reach: a flower, a glass of water, a sweet, even a leaf. Hold it before your shrine, or just in front of you.
Make your own sankalpa, in your own words: your name, today's date, and what you're offering it for. Then offer it, the way Kannappa did, with whatever you have.
If you don't pray, say your name and one thing you'll give your whole heart to today, and set the thing down gently.

wordCard.voice: Pujari. The temple priest: he keeps the rites exact, and offers on your behalf, with your name inside. Today's word.
